## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

72	
73	The contradiction:
74	- `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:154-155`, the team's Example 1: "For any floating-point parameter, a decimal integer literal argument may be used".
75	- The rung's new text restricts that coercion: "ℝ64 coerces from ℤ32, and from every integer numeral whose value ℤ32 holds" (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:43`; the same at `conversions-coercions.tex:64-68`, `:81`, and `changes.tex:448`, `:934-935`).
76	- The list's L2 wrongly records Example 1 as agreeing (`probes/list.txt`, L2).
77	
78	The skeptic would keep the restriction and add a callout saying that a numeral outside ℤ32 no longer converts. That makes the interpreter's representation the standard, against rule 4 of the brief. The decisions settle the point the other way:
79	
80	- **Answer 8** (`POSITIONS.md:159`): "`ZZ32` and integer literals coerce into `RR64` (exact)."
81	- **T's own brief** says that after this batch "only `ZZ32` and numerals convert automatically" (`CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 3, T, "What it writes").
82	- **The rung's own rationale** says "the decision names ℤ32 and the numerals" (`changes.tex:938-939`) and "declared from ℤ32 and the numerals only" (`:467`).
83	- **Rung F's table** gives the restriction only as the effect of `RR64`'s `coerce(x: ZZ32)` **under walk**: "`RR64` from `ZZ32`, which under walk is also every numeral that fits it" (`CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 3, F, "The coercions"). Walk gives a numeral inside ℤ32's range an `Int` and a larger one a `Long` or a big integer (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-56`).
84	- **The language's model:**
85	  - A numeral has a type of its own, and the libraries define the coercions from it (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:126-148`).
86	  - The compiled checker gives every numeral one type whatever its value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:466-467`).
87	  - The team's prelude declares `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` once on each integer type (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:104`, `:148`, `:211`, `:274`, `:333`).
88	  - In that model, "ℝ64 coerces from integer numerals" is one declaration covering every numeral, not a range.

90	So the normative sentences follow answer 8's words: ℝ64 coerces from ℤ32 and from integer numerals. Example 1 then stays true and unchanged.

8	The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) encompasses all finite integers,

20	\\

22	\\
23	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\STR{NN32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit unsigned binary form.

3	== Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:13-878
4	
5	The operator \EXP{\div} performs truncating integer division; if the quotient is
6	not an exact integer, the result is rounded toward zero.
7	
8	The operator \OPR{REM} returns the remainder that would be left over from a division
9	using the operator \EXP{\div}.
10	
11	The operator \OPR{MOD} returns the remainder that would be left over from an integer division
12	that rounds inexact results towards negative infinity (``floor division'').
13	
14	The operator \OPR{DIVREM} returns a tuple of two results, the quotient and remainder
15	from a truncating integer division.
16	
17	The operator \OPR{DIVMOD} returns a tuple of two results, the quotient and remainder
18	from an integer floor division.
19	
20	For all these operators, if \VAR{other} is zero then an \TYP{IntegerDivisionByZero} is thrown.
21	
22	Examples:

34	when the two operands are of opposite sign and their quotient is not an exact integer.

82	\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{LCM}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
83	
84	The operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common divisor of its two arguments.
85	The result is always nonnegative.  If either argment is \EXP{0}, the result
86	equals the other argument.
87	
88	The operator \OPR{LCM} computes the least common multiple of its two arguments.
89	The result is always nonnegative.  If either argment is \EXP{1}, the result
90	equals the other argument.  If either argument is \EXP{0}, the result is \EXP{0}.
91	
92	The strictly positive integers form a partial order and lattice with
93	the ``evenly divides'' operator \EXP{\mid} as the partial order operator and
94	with \OPR{GCD} and \OPR{LCM} as the lattice operators.

258	on the two's-complement representation of the integer;

268	with bits numbered in ``little-endian order'' (least significant bit is bit number 0,
269	least significant bit but one is bit number 1, and so on), then this functional
270	method returns bit \VAR{k} of this representation.

5	\section{Coercion Resolution}
6	\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
7	For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
8	declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
9	specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
10	explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
11	possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
12	chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
13	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
14	declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
15	there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.
16	
17	We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
18	Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
19	\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.
20	
21	For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
22	and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
23	from excludes $U$:
24	\[
25	T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
26	\]
27	Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.
28	
29	We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
30	\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
31	coerced to, and rejects $U$:
32	\[
33	T \morespecificeq U \iff
34	T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
35	(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
36	\]
37	
38	The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
39	necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
40	three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
41	to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
42	this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
43	$T \not\morespecificeq V$.
44	
45	Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
46	between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
47	the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
48	relation elementwise.
49	
50	We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
51	\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.
52	
53	We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
54	declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
55	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
56	Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
57	specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
58	\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
59	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
60	Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
61	a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
62	\Qs)$.
63	
64	Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
65	call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
66	for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.
67	
68	Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
69	the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
70	applicable to the call.
71	Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
72	functional declarations of $\f$ that are
73	applicable with coercion to the call.
74	If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
75	described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
76	element of $\Sigma$ is called.
77	If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
78	follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
79	\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
80	specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
81	$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
82	given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
83	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
84	exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
85	rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
86	\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
87	and the declaration with parameter
88	type $T$ is applied to the call.
89	
90	As an example, consider the following definitions:
91	%trait ZZ32 end
92	%trait ZZ64
93	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
94	%end
95	%trait ZZ128
96	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
97	%  coerce(z:ZZ64) = ...
98	%end
99	%
100	%f(z:ZZ64) = 1
101	%f(z:ZZ128) = 2
102	\begin{Fortress}
103	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{end}\)\\
104	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64\)\\
105	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
106	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
107	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
108	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
109	\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
110	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
111	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
112	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
113	\end{Fortress}
114	Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
115	declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
116	\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the fact that
117	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
118	
119	Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
120	statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
121	into the call.
122	This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
123	
124	For example, in the following program:
125	%trait A
126	%  coerce(c:C) = ...
127	%end
128	%trait B excludes A end
129	%trait C end
130	%object D extends {B,C} end
131	%
132	%f(a:A) = 3
133	%f(b:B) = 4
134	%
135	%c : C = D
136	%f(c)
137	\begin{Fortress}
138	\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
139	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
140	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
141	\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
142	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
143	\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
144	\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
145	\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
146	\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
147	\(f(c)\)
148	\end{Fortress}
149	the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
150	%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
151	\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
152	%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
153	\EXP{f(B)} is
154	%dynamically directly
155	applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
156	coercion.

160	\subsection{GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators}
161	
162	The infix operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common
163	divisor of its integer operands, and \OPR{LCM} computes the least
164	common multiple.  The operator \OPR{CHOOSE} computes binomial
165	coefficients:
166	\EXP{n \OPR{CHOOSE} k = \binom{n}{k} = { n! \over k!(n-k)! }}.
167	
168	The expression \EXP{e \neq e'} is semantically equivalent to the expression
169	\EXP{\neg(e = e')}.

173	\subsection{Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators}
174	
175	For most integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions,
176	multiplication can be expressed using any of `\EXP{\cdot}' or
177	`\EXP{\times}' or simply juxtaposition.
178	However,
179	the \EXP{\times} operator is used to
180	express the shape of matrices, so if expressions using multiplication are used
181	in expressing the shape of a matrix, it may be necessary to avoid the
182	use of '\EXP{\times}' to
183	express multiplication, or to use parentheses.
184	
185	For integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions, division is expressed by \EXP{/}.
186	When the operator \EXP{/} is used to divide one integer by another,
187	the result is rational.
188	The operator \EXP{\div} performs truncating integer division:
189	\EXP{m \div n = \mathit{signum}\left({m \over n}\right) \left\lfloor \left| {m \over n} \right| \right\rfloor}.
190	The operator \OPR{REM} gives the remainder from such a truncating division:
191	\EXP{m \OPR{REM} n = m - n (m \div n)}.
192	The operator \OPR{MOD} gives the remainder from a floor division:
193	\EXP{m \OPR{MOD} n = m - n \left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor};
194	when \EXP{n>0} this is the usual modulus computation that evaluates integer \VAR{m}
195	to an integer \VAR{k} such that \EXP{0\leq{}k<n} and \VAR{n} evenly divides \EXP{m-k}.
196	
197	The special operators \OPR{DIVREM} and \OPR{DIVMOD} each return a pair of values,
198	the quotient and the remainder; \EXP{m \OPR{DIVREM} n} returns
199	\EXP{(m \div n, m \OPR{REM} n)} while
200	\EXP{m \OPR{DIVMOD} n} returns
201	\EXP{(\left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor, m \OPR{MOD} n)}.
202	
203	Multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is done with juxtaposition,
204	as is multiplication of a vector by a matrix (on either side).  Vector dot product
205	is expressed by `\EXP{\cdot}' and vector cross product by
206	`\EXP{\times}'.  Division of
207	a matrix or vector by a scalar may be expressed using `\EXP{/}'.
208	
209	The syntactic interaction of juxtaposition, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{\times},
210	and \EXP{/} is subtle.
211	\See{operator-precedence} for a discussion of the relative precedence of
212	these operations and how precedence may depend on the use of whitespace.
213	
214	The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
215	For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
216	Rational computations do not overflow.
217	For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
218	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
219	For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.
220	
221	Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
222	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
223	
224	The handling of division by zero depends on the type of the number produced.
225	For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
226	For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
227	For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
228	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
229	For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
230	(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).
231	
232	Wraparound multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
233	\EXP{\dottimes}.
234	Saturating multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
235	\EXP{\boxdot} or \EXP{\boxtimes}.
236	These operations do not overflow.
237	
238	Ordinary multiplication and division of floating-point numbers always
239	use the IEEE 754 ``round to nearest'' rounding mode.  This rounding
240	mode may be emphasized by using the operators \EXP{\otimes} (or \EXP{\odot})
241	and \EXP{\oslash}.  Multiplication and division in ``round toward zero''
242	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\boxtimes} (or \EXP{\boxdot}) and
243	\EXP{\boxslash}.
244	Multiplication and division in ``round toward positive infinity''
245	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\uptimes} (or \EXP{\updot}) and \EXP{\upslash}.
246	Multiplication and division in ``round toward negative infinity''
247	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downtimes} (or \EXP{\downdot}) and
248	\EXP{\downslash}.

441	## 2. The one reading everything rational rests on
442	
443	The original design has three rational value sets, ℚ (finite), ℚ\* (with ±∞) and ℚ# (with 0/0), and puts each in a type. Answer 6 rewrites the subtype lists "as the library's run-time check methods (`check`/`check_star`, returning `Maybe`)" (`POSITIONS.md:158`). That is the library's model: one wide type, refined at run time. `RR64` holds the infinities and NaN, and `check` and `check_star` pick out its finite and its non-NaN values (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:301-304`; bodies `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:395-399`). The library's one rational type `QQ` is wide in the same way: `Ratio(1,0)`, `Ratio(-1,0)` and `Ratio(0,0)` are values of it (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:628-631`, made by the integer division at `:953-960`), and `QQ` declares `isNaN`, `isInfinite` and `isFinite` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:393-396`). Measured under walk on the base (`probes/examples/RatValues.walk.txt`): `1/0 is 1/0, isInfinite true`; `0/0 is 0/0, isNaN true`; `1/0 + -1/0 is 0/0`; `typecase 1/0 of QQ: QQ`; `check` on `1/0` gives `Nothing` and `check_star` on `0/0` gives `Nothing`. The compiled path has no `QQ` (its prelude is flat and has none; `CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 3, F, "For the skeptic"), so there is no second path to run. The specification already says the same in its operator chapter: "For rational results, division by zero produces 1/0" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:166`; the first wording of this record cited `:182-183`, corrected in the repair round, `JUDGE.md` section 1.3).
444	
445	So the one type ℚ holds the finite rationals, +∞, −∞ and 0/0; the refinements the original expressed by ℚ and ℚ\* are the run-time checks answer 6 names. If ℚ held only the finite rationals, the two checks would have nothing to refine and the library's rational type would contradict the chapter. This is the rung's reading of answer 6, taken as settled; section 5 states the alternative and why it is not taken.
446	
447	The integers are the other way round: the library's integer types hold no infinity (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:647-648`, "For now, no infinite integers"), and the operator chapter's integer division by zero throws (`opr-overview.tex:165`; first cited as `:181`). The original's ℤ\* has no counterpart.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
Union$RTTIc.class

content.content:
## Hard rules

These are not judgement calls.

- Pavol decides what gets committed. A batch run and a Fable worker wait for
  his yes, each time. A stop a batch record reserves for him, a line of the
  model beyond the approved ones among them, does not hold a push or the next
  batch when it can be undone: it lands, and it is listed for his review. Standing approval covers only the approved ladder in
  `modernization-plan.md` and the push order below. A step his yes already
  covers is taken, not asked about again.
- Never committed: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable,
  Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck (`research/decks/` is gitignored;
  cite by Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief
  attributed quotations); HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without his go. His email
  is for attribution only.
- Every push: `git push origin main`, then
  `git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8`; no other branch
  without permission (the transcript orphan branches excepted). Commit footer,
  exactly:

  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
  ```

- A worker commits only the paths it wrote, as it goes, in one command
  (`git add -- <paths> && git commit -m … -- <paths>`), never a directory
  copy, and pushes only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing but its
  own commits; the coordinator reviews after and fixes by a further commit. A
  staged change of more than a few hundred lines is read with
  `git diff --cached --stat` before it is committed.
- The gate: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` with zero
  failures, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression; the checker
  count reported, never red on its own. Every edit under the original tree is
  test first, the test seen failing before the fix, and is flagged at commit.
- Never the AskUserQuestion dialog; options go in plain text.

## Principles

**1. We are custodians of their language, not its authors.** Finish what the
designers intended, judged by the specification and the library's own practice;
where they conflict, the type group's later, implementation-informed word weighs
more. So: no self-credit anywhere committed, attribution reconstructed where git
does not record it, provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports
rather than source comments, every claim verified against a primary source. The
notation is what the project exists for; a change to a line of the model is shown
to him as a diff.

**2. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches him.**
What the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the
specification says under every spelling; what the library already does in the
same family and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what
the commits say; then the derivation from his principles and the decision in
his words. Solutions are the language's and the library's, not the first two
someone wrote down: a brief states the problem and never the expected answer, a
worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language offers before a
fork reaches him, and a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the
library gets around it. When something goes wrong or is undecided, the answer
is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch.
One variable per step; reproduce before explaining; a timing names the machine
it ran on (`nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK,
`FORTRESS_THREADS`), and only a pair taken in one run measures a difference.

**3. He carries the responsibility, so his attention is the scarcest thing we
spend.** He reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time. One ask per
message, in this order: the question in one line; the context in short bullets,
